sections.guidingQuestion: Which neuronal structure commonly conducts action potentials over long distances?
sections.explanation:
Neurons have a cell body containing the nucleus and cytoplasm. Multiple branched dendrites commonly receive inputs, whereas a single long axon conducts action potentials toward terminal branches. Neurons vary greatly in shape and axon length according to their roles.

The membranes of these cells contain ion channels and pumps that allow changes in voltage to carry information along nerve fibres. At terminals, electrical activity may initiate chemical signalling to another neuron, muscle or gland.

Dendrites create a large surface area for receiving signals from receptor cells or other neurons, while the cell body integrates incoming information and maintains the cell. The axon is an elongated membrane-bound fibre; a travelling impulse reaches its terminal branches, where communication to the next cell can begin. Myelin, when present, electrically insulates much of the axon and helps increase conduction speed. A nerve is not one giant neuron: it is a bundle of fibres from numerous neurons. Follow the normal route of information from a receiving region through the cell body and axon to the terminal, while recognizing that sensory-neuron shapes may differ from the familiar multipolar textbook diagram.

sections.guidingQuestion: What directly sustains Na⁺ and K⁺ concentration gradients over time?
sections.explanation:
At rest a neuron typically maintains more Na⁺ outside and more K⁺ inside its plasma membrane. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase hydrolyses ATP to move three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in per pumping cycle, both against their electrochemical gradients.

Potassium leak conductance, impermeant intracellular anions and ion gradients help leave the inside negative relative to the outside (often approximately −70 mV in illustrative neurons). Pumps maintain the gradients over time; they do not alone cause every moment of membrane voltage.

The sodium–potassium pump hydrolyses ATP to export three Na⁺ ions and import two K⁺ ions per cycle, maintaining high Na⁺ concentration outside and high K⁺ concentration inside the neuron. At rest, the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺ because of open potassium leak channels. K⁺ diffuses outward down its concentration gradient, leaving the inside relatively negative; an increasing electrical attraction opposes further loss of K⁺. The resting potential therefore reflects selective permeability and ion gradients, with a smaller direct electrogenic contribution from the pump. Polarization means a voltage difference across a membrane, not that the neuron has become electrically charged throughout its entire length.

sections.guidingQuestion: What carries the local current involved in nerve impulses?
sections.explanation:
An action potential is a brief regenerative change in membrane voltage caused by ion currents. It is electrical because charged ions move across the axonal membrane, changing the voltage difference between the cytoplasm and extracellular fluid.

Once initiated, the action potential propagates along an axon without continuously decreasing in amplitude under normal conditions; energy is needed to maintain ion gradients across many impulses, not to physically carry electrons down the axon.

A nerve impulse is a travelling change in membrane potential, rather than sodium ions flowing from one end of an axon all the way to the other. Depolarization in one region alters the voltage of nearby membrane; in an excitable region this stimulates a new action potential. Positive ions moving across the membrane account for the electrical nature of the signal. The action potential is regenerated along the fibre and so does not gradually diminish like a passive voltage change. At this shared SL/HL level, the essential ideas are membrane voltage, ion movement and propagation; the specific timing of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels is an additional HL mechanism.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which change typically increases conduction speed?
sections.explanation:
Greater axon diameter reduces internal electrical resistance and tends to increase conduction speed. The squid giant axon provides a classic example of increased speed by large diameter despite lacking vertebrate-style myelin; thinner unmyelinated fibres usually conduct more slowly.

Myelin electrically insulates internodes and allows impulses to regenerate at nodes, producing much faster conduction than similarly sized unmyelinated fibres. When interpreting data, distinguish a positive diameter–velocity correlation from a causal mechanism, and use r or R² only for appropriately documented datasets. In a clearly hypothetical simple linear regression with an intercept, r = +0.80 indicates a positive linear relationship and R² = 0.64 means the fitted model explains 64% of the observed variation in conduction speed. Neither statistic by itself demonstrates causation; report speed in m s⁻¹.

A larger axon diameter lowers internal resistance to local current spread, so the next membrane segment can reach excitation more quickly. Giant squid axons illustrate rapid conduction without myelin; narrow unmyelinated fibres conduct more slowly. Myelinated fibres conduct especially rapidly because current spreads beneath the insulating sheath and impulses are regenerated mainly at exposed nodes. In data analysis, a positive correlation coefficient r means both measured variables tend to increase together; a negative r means one tends to decrease as the other increases. For an example r = +0.80, R² = 0.64: a fitted linear model explains 64% of the observed variation in speed. R² neither proves causation nor means that 64% of individual axons follow the model exactly.

sections.guidingQuestion: What makes a typical chemical synapse directional?
sections.explanation:
A chemical synapse has a presynaptic terminal, a narrow synaptic cleft and a postsynaptic membrane with receptors. At a typical synapse neurotransmitter vesicles are concentrated presynaptically while transmitter-sensitive receptors are located postsynaptically.

Because secretion and detection are arranged asymmetrically, signalling normally crosses this junction in one direction. Synapses can join two neurons or a neuron and an effector such as a muscle cell.

A typical chemical synapse separates a transmitting presynaptic terminal from a receiving postsynaptic membrane by a narrow cleft. The presynaptic terminal stores transmitter in vesicles and releases it on stimulation, whereas the postsynaptic membrane bears the relevant receptors. Transmitter molecules diffuse across the cleft, bind receptors and alter the receiving cell's activity. This anatomical asymmetry explains why information normally passes from the releasing to the receiving cell rather than spontaneously in reverse. Such junctions connect neurons to other neurons and also to effectors including muscles and glands. Do not confuse the electrical impulse travelling along an axon with the chemical message crossing a synaptic cleft.

sections.guidingQuestion: What ion enters the terminal and triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis?

sections.guidingQuestion: What is an excitatory postsynaptic potential?
sections.explanation:
Released acetylcholine diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds suitable postsynaptic ligand-gated receptors. At the neuromuscular junction nicotinic acetylcholine receptor channels open, permitting cation movement with net positive charge entry near the resting potential.

The postsynaptic voltage becomes less negative: this graded depolarization is an excitatory postsynaptic potential or end-plate potential. If sufficient depolarization reaches an excitable membrane's threshold, a new action potential may be initiated.

Acetylcholine released at a chemical synapse moves through the cleft by diffusion and binds a transmembrane receptor on the receiving cell. Where the receptor opens a cation channel, the resulting inward positive current makes the postsynaptic membrane less negative. This graded change is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP), not necessarily a full action potential. If enough depolarization reaches the trigger region and the threshold is crossed, an action potential can begin in the postsynaptic neuron. Acetylcholine acts at many types of synapse, notably at neuromuscular junctions, where the receiving membrane belongs to a muscle cell. Signal duration is limited by removal or breakdown of transmitter, so binding is not permanent.

sections.guidingQuestion: Which ion current principally drives the rapid upstroke?
sections.explanation:
When membrane depolarization reaches threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels rapidly open. Na⁺ enters, creating a steep rising phase and often briefly making the inside positive; Na⁺ channels then inactivate.

Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open more slowly; outward K⁺ current repolarizes the membrane and may cause an after-hyperpolarization before resting voltage is re-established. Channel inactivation and delayed recovery contribute to the refractory period.

A stimulus first depolarizes an excitable membrane toward threshold. At threshold enough voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open to create positive feedback: Na⁺ enters, driving a rapid rising phase and often a brief reversal of membrane polarity. Na⁺ channels then inactivate while slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels open; K⁺ leaves and repolarizes the membrane. Because K⁺ conductance can remain elevated after the main falling phase, membrane potential may briefly undershoot resting voltage before returning to baseline. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains the longer-term concentration gradients but does not directly produce the rapid millisecond falling phase. Distinguish threshold, rising phase, peak, repolarization and after-hyperpolarization on a labelled trace.

sections.guidingQuestion: What allows an action potential to move along the axon?
sections.explanation:
At one active region Na⁺ entry makes intracellular charge less negative, producing local current that spreads into adjacent resting axon. This current depolarizes the next membrane region to threshold and opens its voltage-gated sodium channels.

The regenerative wave advances along the axon. Sodium-channel inactivation behind the wave creates a refractory region, helping prevent immediate backward re-excitation under ordinary physiological conditions.

When a small patch of axon membrane depolarizes, Na⁺ entry makes its cytoplasm more positive than nearby resting regions. Positive charge spreads longitudinally inside the axon toward the less positive region, with return current outside the membrane. The local circuit depolarizes an adjacent excitable segment; if that segment reaches threshold, it opens its own voltage-gated Na⁺ channels and regenerates the action potential. The region just behind the advancing wave is temporarily refractory because many Na⁺ channels are inactivated, making immediate backward re-excitation unlikely. Consequently, the impulse advances while each membrane patch undergoes its own rise and fall in voltage. Directional propagation is not the movement of a fixed parcel of Na⁺ down the entire axon.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the frequency of five action potentials in 0.25 s?
sections.explanation:
An oscilloscope trace of membrane potential plots voltage, typically in millivolts (mV), against time, typically milliseconds (ms). A resting baseline is negative, an action potential shows a rapid depolarization and repolarization, and after-hyperpolarization can dip below baseline.

Count discrete action-potential peaks during a defined observation interval to calculate frequency: number of impulses divided by elapsed time in seconds, giving hertz (Hz). Increasing stimulus intensity often changes spike frequency rather than spike height.

An oscilloscope recording plots membrane potential (mV) vertically against time (ms or s) horizontally. Identify a baseline near the resting potential, a rise once threshold is reached, a positive peak, a fall and sometimes an after-hyperpolarization. The trace corresponds to sequential channel states in the membrane, not to the shape of the whole neuron. To calculate firing frequency, count completed action potentials in a specified time window and divide count by elapsed seconds: five impulses in 0.25 s gives 5 ÷ 0.25 = 20 impulses s⁻¹ (20 Hz). Greater stimulus intensity often changes spike frequency rather than the amplitude of individual all-or-nothing action potentials. Always check axis units before converting milliseconds to seconds.

sections.guidingQuestion: Where are action potentials regenerated along a myelinated axon?
sections.explanation:
Schwann cells or oligodendrocytes form myelin around axon segments, leaving exposed nodes of Ranvier. Nodes contain high densities of voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; the current spreads rapidly under the insulating myelin to depolarize the next node.

New action potentials are regenerated at successive nodes rather than every small length of membrane. This saltatory pattern greatly increases speed and can reduce ionic pumping costs for a given propagation distance.

In a myelinated axon, multiple membrane wraps reduce ion leakage and change electrical properties of the internodal membrane. sections.guidingQuestion: How does cocaine chiefly modify monoamine synaptic signalling?
sections.explanation:
Exogenous compounds can change neurotransmission by binding receptors or altering transmitter clearance. Neonicotinoids are insecticides that bind insect nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and disrupt normal cholinergic transmission, typically by persistent receptor activation and subsequent functional impairment.

sections.guidingQuestion: What is the typical effect of an IPSP?
sections.explanation:
An inhibitory neurotransmitter can increase postsynaptic conductance to ions such as Cl⁻ or K⁺, generally making the membrane voltage more negative or stabilizing it below excitation threshold. The resulting inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) lowers the likelihood of an action potential.

For example, activation of some GABA receptors increases chloride conductance in mature neurons. The precise voltage effect depends on the ion gradients; shunting inhibition can reduce excitation without a large visible hyperpolarization.

An inhibitory neurotransmitter binds a receptor that raises conductance to ions such as Cl⁻ or K⁺ in the postsynaptic membrane. Depending on the ion gradients, this can shift voltage to a more negative level or stabilize the membrane close to a negative ion equilibrium potential. The resulting inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) makes excitation less likely because depolarizing inputs must overcome the inhibitory effect to reach the action-potential threshold. The IPSP is a graded local event; it is not an action potential travelling backward. In a simplified trace, draw the resting baseline and show an inhibitory deflection below it. In living neurons, some inhibition is also shunting, reducing the effect of concurrent excitation without a large visible voltage fall.

Each excitatory or inhibitory input causes a graded postsynaptic voltage change. Spatial summation combines inputs arriving at different synapses within a short interval; temporal summation combines closely spaced inputs at the same synapse.

At the axon initial segment the net effects of depolarizing and inhibiting inputs determine whether threshold is reached. An action potential is all-or-nothing once threshold is crossed, even though contributing postsynaptic potentials have variable size.

One postsynaptic neuron may receive many chemical synapses. EPSPs from different presynaptic terminals can overlap (spatial summation), and repeated EPSPs from the same terminal can overlap before an earlier potential has decayed (temporal summation). IPSPs counteract or shunt this excitatory effect. The combined membrane voltage at the axon trigger region determines whether threshold is reached: below threshold no action potential is initiated, whereas crossing threshold produces an all-or-nothing impulse. This explains how a network can integrate many small inputs into a single output decision. Draw separate incoming EPSPs and IPSPs and then the resulting voltage; do not simply count the number of excitatory synapses without considering their timing and strength.

sections.guidingQuestion: What directly starts excitation of a capsaicin-sensitive free nerve ending?
sections.explanation:
Free nerve endings in the skin can act as nociceptors. Receptor channels responding to potentially damaging heat, acidic conditions or capsaicin open and allow inward positive ion current, producing a generator potential.

If the depolarization reaches threshold the sensory neuron fires action potentials. Neural pathways carry information to the central nervous system, and perception of pain arises through processing in the brain rather than within the skin ending itself.

Free sensory nerve endings in skin can detect potentially damaging heat, acidity and capsaicin from chilli peppers. Stimulus-sensitive ion channels open and admit positive charge, producing a local depolarizing receptor potential. When this brings the excitable sensory membrane to threshold, action potentials propagate toward the central nervous system. Further neural pathways carry and process the information in the brain, where the conscious experience of pain emerges. Distinguish transduction at the nerve ending from conduction along the sensory fibre and subsequent perception. A receptor potential varies in size with stimulation; the resulting action potentials remain all-or-nothing, with stimulus strength represented partly by their frequency and recruitment.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is consciousness classified as emergent?
sections.explanation:
An individual neuron can generate impulses and communicate with its neighbours, but no single neuron has all the properties of conscious experience. Networks of interconnected neurons integrate sensory information, attention and internal states across distributed brain systems.

Consciousness is described as an emergent property because it depends on coordinated interactions at the network scale. The complete neuronal explanation of subjective awareness remains an active research question; this curriculum concept does not require asserting one settled theory.

A single neuron can generate action potentials and form synapses, but it cannot by itself account for the integrated experiences described as consciousness. Populations of neurons combine sensory information with stored memories, attention and other ongoing activity through interconnected pathways. Large-scale patterns of communication permit functions that are absent at the scale of an isolated cell. Consciousness is therefore presented as an emergent property of interacting neural systems rather than a special chemical produced by one neuron. This does not imply that every detail of consciousness is fully explained. The syllabus point is an example of systems biology: interacting parts generate new capacities at a higher level of organization.

recall.prompt: Explain consciousness as an emergent property with a mechanism and outcome.
recall.answer:
An individual neuron can generate impulses and communicate with its neighbours, but no single neuron has all the properties of conscious experience. Networks of interconnected neurons integrate sensory information, attention and internal states across distributed brain systems.

Consciousness is described as an emergent property because it depends on coordinated interactions at the network scale. The complete neuronal explanation of subjective awareness remains an active research question; this curriculum concept does not require asserting one settled theory.

A single neuron can generate action potentials and form synapses, but it cannot by itself account for the integrated experiences described as consciousness. Populations of neurons combine sensory information with stored memories, attention and other ongoing activity through interconnected pathways. Large-scale patterns of communication permit functions that are absent at the scale of an isolated cell. Consciousness is therefore presented as an emergent property of interacting neural systems rather than a special chemical produced by one neuron. This does not imply that every detail of consciousness is fully explained. The syllabus point is an example of systems biology: interacting parts generate new capacities at a higher level of organization.

questions.prompt: Which neuronal structure commonly conducts action potentials over long distances?

options.feedback: A neuron's axon conducts action potentials toward synaptic terminals.
The nucleus contains the genome; it does not act as the long impulse-conducting fibre.
Dendritic spines receive synaptic input, but an axon typically conducts impulses over long distances.
The Golgi apparatus processes cellular products rather than conducting propagated action potentials.

questions.prompt: Explain neuron structure and function, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: The membranes of these cells contain ion channels and pumps that allow changes in voltage to carry information along nerve fibres. At terminals, electrical activity may initiate chemical signalling to another neuron, muscle or gland. A sensory neuron can carry information from a heat receptor in skin toward the central nervous system.
markingPoints: The membranes of these cells contain ion channels and pumps that allow changes in voltage to carry information along nerve fibres. At terminals, electrical activity may initiate chemical signalling to another neuron, muscle or gland.

questions.prompt: What directly sustains Na⁺ and K⁺ concentration gradients over time?

options.feedback: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase hydrolyses ATP while exporting Na⁺ and importing K⁺.
Oxygen diffusion does not perform ATP-powered ion transport against gradients.
Transcription can produce ion-pump proteins but does not directly move Na⁺ or K⁺ across the membrane.
Exocytosis exports vesicle cargo, not the ongoing ion exchange that maintains resting gradients.

questions.prompt: Explain the sodium-potassium pump and resting potential, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Potassium leak conductance, impermeant intracellular anions and ion gradients help leave the inside negative relative to the outside (often approximately −70 mV in illustrative neurons). Pumps maintain the gradients over time; they do not alone cause every moment of membrane voltage. If ATP production stops for long enough, ion gradients erode and normal excitability is lost.

questions.prompt: What carries the local current involved in nerve impulses?

options.text: Movement of ions such as Na⁺ and K⁺
options.feedback: Ionic movement across and along membranes, rather than free-electron flow, carries neuronal current.

options.text: Free electrons flowing down cytoplasm like a copper wire
options.feedback: Axons conduct through ion movements and changing membrane voltage, unlike electrons moving in metal wire.
DNA does not shuttle along nerve fibres to transmit each electrical signal.
ATP production supports pumps indirectly; moving ATP vesicles does not constitute the electrical impulse.

questions.prompt: Explain action potentials as electrical nerve impulses, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Once initiated, the action potential propagates along an axon without continuously decreasing in amplitude under normal conditions; energy is needed to maintain ion gradients across many impulses, not to physically carry electrons down the axon. An impulse can travel from a neuron's initial segment to its synaptic terminal.

questions.prompt: Which change typically increases conduction speed?

options.text: Increasing axon diameter while other factors remain comparable
options.feedback: Wider axons generally have lower internal resistance and faster conduction, all else equal.
Narrower axons normally increase axial resistance and slow conduction relative to comparable wider fibres.

options.text: Removing myelin from a healthy fibre
options.feedback: Myelin reduces current loss and speeds saltatory conduction; removing it typically slows propagation.
Voltage-gated channels at nodes are necessary for regenerative impulses, not obstacles to speed.

questions.prompt: Explain axon diameter, myelin and transmission speed, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Myelin electrically insulates internodes and allows impulses to regenerate at nodes, producing much faster conduction than similarly sized unmyelinated fibres. When interpreting data, distinguish a positive diameter–velocity correlation from a causal mechanism, and use r or R² only for appropriately documented datasets. Comparing two axons of similar diameter, the myelinated axon usually transmits impulses faster.

questions.prompt: What makes a typical chemical synapse directional?

options.text: Presynaptic release machinery faces postsynaptic transmitter receptors
options.feedback: Presynaptic vesicle release and postsynaptic receptors establish typical one-way synaptic transmission.

options.text: The axon lacks a plasma membrane
options.feedback: An axon requires a plasma membrane with ion channels to conduct an action potential.

options.text: Both cells must release transmitter simultaneously
options.feedback: A typical chemical synapse does not need both cells to release transmitter at the same time.

options.text: The cleft is filled with DNA
options.feedback: The cleft contains extracellular fluid across which transmitter diffuses, not a DNA bridge.

questions.prompt: Explain chemical synapses and directional transfer, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Because secretion and detection are arranged asymmetrically, signalling normally crosses this junction in one direction. Synapses can join two neurons or a neuron and an effector such as a muscle cell. A motor neuron communicates to a muscle fibre at a neuromuscular junction.
markingPoints: Because secretion and detection are arranged asymmetrically, signalling normally crosses this junction in one direction. Synapses can join two neurons or a neuron and an effector such as a muscle cell.
A motor neuron communicates to a muscle fibre at a neuromuscular junction.

questions.prompt: What ion enters the terminal and triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis?

options.feedback: Ca²⁺ enters via voltage-gated channels and triggers vesicle fusion at the presynaptic terminal.
Chloride movement can modify membrane potential, but Ca²⁺ is the principal exocytosis trigger.
Molecular oxygen is not a calcium-like charged signalling ion that directly triggers vesicle fusion.
DNA is a macromolecule and does not pass through presynaptic calcium channels.

questions.prompt: Explain calcium-triggered neurotransmitter release, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Vesicles merge with the presynaptic membrane and release transmitter by exocytosis into the cleft. Neurotransmitter release therefore depends on voltage-gated calcium entry rather than direct movement of neurotransmitter through the axon membrane. Removing external calcium strongly reduces evoked neurotransmitter exocytosis.
markingPoints: Vesicles merge with the presynaptic membrane and release transmitter by exocytosis into the cleft. Neurotransmitter release therefore depends on voltage-gated calcium entry rather than direct movement of neurotransmitter through the axon membrane.

questions.prompt: What is an excitatory postsynaptic potential?

options.text: A graded depolarization that increases action-potential likelihood
options.feedback: An EPSP is a small graded depolarization that makes reaching threshold more likely.

options.text: An obligatory negative shift far below rest
options.feedback: A negative shift below rest is characteristic of hyperpolarization, not an excitatory depolarization.

options.text: A DNA copy generated after every synapse
options.feedback: Synaptic transmission changes membrane conductance rapidly; it does not require copying DNA each time.

options.text: Movement of insulin into the nucleus
options.feedback: Insulin nuclear transport is unrelated to the graded electrical response at an excitatory synapse.

questions.prompt: Explain excitatory postsynaptic potentials, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: The postsynaptic voltage becomes less negative: this graded depolarization is an excitatory postsynaptic potential or end-plate potential. If sufficient depolarization reaches an excitable membrane's threshold, a new action potential may be initiated. A small EPSP might not reach threshold alone but can contribute to a larger summed depolarization.
markingPoints: The postsynaptic voltage becomes less negative: this graded depolarization is an excitatory postsynaptic potential or end-plate potential. If sufficient depolarization reaches an excitable membrane's threshold, a new action potential may be initiated.

questions.prompt: Which ion current principally drives the rapid upstroke?

options.feedback: Opening voltage-gated Na⁺ channels generates the rapid depolarizing current.
ATP synthase is not a potassium-entry channel; K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated channels helps repolarize.
Steroid receptors regulate signalling or transcription, not the action-potential sodium upstroke.
GLUT4 transports glucose and is not an electrogenic channel for the fast upstroke.

questions.prompt: Explain voltage-gated channels and the action-potential phases, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels open more slowly; outward K⁺ current repolarizes the membrane and may cause an after-hyperpolarization before resting voltage is re-established. Channel inactivation and delayed recovery contribute to the refractory period. A schematic trace rises sharply from about −70 mV to positive values, then falls and transiently undershoots rest.

questions.prompt: What allows an action potential to move along the axon?

options.text: Local currents depolarize adjacent membrane to threshold
options.feedback: Local ionic current depolarizes adjacent axon membrane until voltage-gated channels regenerate the impulse.

options.text: One packet of Na⁺ moves untouched from one end to the other
options.feedback: An impulse is renewed in successive membrane regions; the identical ions do not travel the entire axon.

options.text: Glucose channels open in every region
options.feedback: Glucose transport is not the event that regenerates neighbouring membrane action potentials.

options.text: Neurotransmitter diffuses inside the whole axon
options.feedback: Neurotransmitters diffuse across synapses, not as the propagating electrical carrier inside an entire axon.

questions.prompt: Explain local currents and impulse propagation, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: The regenerative wave advances along the axon. Sodium-channel inactivation behind the wave creates a refractory region, helping prevent immediate backward re-excitation under ordinary physiological conditions. A stimulated mid-axon region can initially send action potentials in both directions, but normal initiation at the axon initial segment propagates toward terminals.
markingPoints: The regenerative wave advances along the axon. Sodium-channel inactivation behind the wave creates a refractory region, helping prevent immediate backward re-excitation under ordinary physiological conditions.
A stimulated mid-axon region can initially send action potentials in both directions, but normal initiation at the axon initial segment propagates toward terminals.

questions.prompt: What is the frequency of five action potentials in 0.25 s?

options.feedback: Frequency is count divided by time: 5 ÷ 0.25 s = 20 impulses s⁻¹ = 20 Hz.
1.25 is the product 5 × 0.25, not impulses divided by elapsed time.
Millivolts measure voltage, whereas frequency requires reciprocal seconds (Hz).
0.05 Hz is not 5/0.25; divide impulse count by the time interval in seconds.

questions.prompt: Explain interpreting voltage traces and firing frequency, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Count discrete action-potential peaks during a defined observation interval to calculate frequency: number of impulses divided by elapsed time in seconds, giving hertz (Hz). Increasing stimulus intensity often changes spike frequency rather than spike height. Five action potentials recorded in 0.25 s correspond to a mean frequency of 20 Hz.

questions.prompt: Where are action potentials regenerated along a myelinated axon?

options.feedback: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels clustered at nodes regenerate action potentials between myelinated segments.
Compact myelin insulates internodes, where the same density of regenerative channels is absent.
The nucleus processes gene expression; it is not an axonal site where impulses regenerate.
Mitochondria help supply ATP, but the action-potential spike is regenerated at nodal membrane.

questions.prompt: Explain saltatory conduction at nodes of ranvier, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: New action potentials are regenerated at successive nodes rather than every small length of membrane. This saltatory pattern greatly increases speed and can reduce ionic pumping costs for a given propagation distance. The electrical signal appears to jump from one node to the next, although local currents flow through the internode.

questions.prompt: How does cocaine chiefly modify monoamine synaptic signalling?

options.feedback: Cocaine inhibits monoamine reuptake transporters, leaving more transmitter in the synaptic space.
Cocaine does not transform dopamine into ATP; the effect concerns membrane uptake of transmitter.

options.text: It blocks every postsynaptic ion channel irreversibly
options.feedback: It does not irreversibly shut every postsynaptic ion channel; its central effect is transporter inhibition.
Changes in myelin thickness are not the acute mechanism of cocaine's synaptic effects.

questions.prompt: Explain exogenous chemicals affecting synapses, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: Cocaine inhibits monoamine neurotransmitter transporters, prominently the dopamine transporter, reducing reuptake of released transmitter. The increased extracellular transmitter prolongs signalling. These are different mechanisms: receptor targeting versus transporter inhibition. Blocking dopamine reuptake can prolong dopamine activity in a synaptic cleft.

questions.prompt: What is the typical effect of an IPSP?

options.text: Reduced likelihood of reaching action-potential threshold
options.feedback: An IPSP usually hyperpolarizes or shunts membrane responses, decreasing firing likelihood.

options.text: Guaranteed extra firing regardless of excitation
options.feedback: Inhibitory signalling reduces, rather than guarantees, reaching threshold after excitation.
Insulin secretion is endocrine physiology, not the direct definition of a postsynaptic inhibitory potential.

options.text: Production of a larger neuron nucleus
options.feedback: Cell-nucleus size does not explain a transient change in postsynaptic membrane potential.

questions.prompt: Explain inhibitory postsynaptic potentials, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: For example, activation of some GABA receptors increases chloride conductance in mature neurons. The precise voltage effect depends on the ion gradients; shunting inhibition can reduce excitation without a large visible hyperpolarization. An inhibitory input can counteract a simultaneous excitatory input at the axon initial segment.
markingPoints: For example, activation of some GABA receptors increases chloride conductance in mature neurons. The precise voltage effect depends on the ion gradients; shunting inhibition can reduce excitation without a large visible hyperpolarization.

questions.prompt: What describes spatial summation?

options.text: Combining signals from different synapses at similar times
options.feedback: Spatial summation combines postsynaptic potentials from several synapses at approximately the same time.

options.text: Repeated signals from one synapse over time
options.feedback: Repeated inputs from one synapse across time illustrate temporal, not spatial, summation.
Sodium pumping into a nucleus is unrelated to integration of inputs at the neuronal membrane.

options.text: A signal crossing a myelin membrane
options.feedback: A signal passing along a myelinated axon is conduction, not summation at synaptic inputs.

questions.prompt: Explain spatial and temporal synaptic summation, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: At the axon initial segment the net effects of depolarizing and inhibiting inputs determine whether threshold is reached. An action potential is all-or-nothing once threshold is crossed, even though contributing postsynaptic potentials have variable size. Two simultaneous EPSPs can reach threshold together; a concurrent IPSP can prevent this.

questions.prompt: What directly starts excitation of a capsaicin-sensitive free nerve ending?

options.feedback: Capsaicin can activate sensory cation channels, depolarizing a free nerve ending.
Liver hormone release is not the direct first event when a cutaneous nerve ending detects capsaicin.

options.text: Myelin synthesis at the skin surface
options.feedback: Myelin production does not transduce a noxious chemical stimulus at the nerve ending.

options.text: Insulin binding to a synaptic vesicle
options.feedback: Insulin-receptor binding is unrelated to the capsaicin-sensitive sensory ion channel.

questions.prompt: Explain nociceptors and pain perception, giving one relevant biological example. [2]
questions.answer: If the depolarization reaches threshold the sensory neuron fires action potentials. Neural pathways carry information to the central nervous system, and perception of pain arises through processing in the brain rather than within the skin ending itself. Capsaicin activates TRPV1 channels in some nociceptors and can produce a burning sensation.

questions.prompt: An oscilloscope trace has six action-potential peaks during a 0.30 s observation window. Their individual heights are approximately +30 mV. Calculate impulse frequency, specify the unit, and explain why a stronger sustained stimulus typically alters frequency rather than spike amplitude. [5]

data.caption: Invented trace summary; approximate positive peak is not an exact universal spike voltage.

questions.answer: Frequency = 6/0.30 s = 20 Hz. Once threshold is reached, a spike is regenerative and approximately all-or-nothing; stimulus intensity can alter spike frequency. The +30 mV value is voltage, not frequency.
markingPoints: Use impulses divided by time.
Calculate 6/0.30 = 20.
Give Hz or s⁻¹ as the unit of frequency.
Voltage-gated channel opening produces regenerative, approximately all-or-nothing action potentials.
